title: What Should You Ask a Web Development Company Before Hiring?
description: Ask a web development company questions that reveal scope, evidence, testing, ownership and support before you approve a project.
summary: Follow a fictional Varanasi music school as it replaces three polished sales calls with an evidence based provider interview and decision record.
body:
What should you ask a web development company before hiring? Ask questions that make the provider show how the project will be scoped, reviewed, tested, handed over and supported. A useful answer should lead to something inspectable: a relevant example, a written boundary, an acceptance check, an account owner or a named next step.

Do not choose from a technology list or a ranking promise alone. First confirm that the company understands the visitor task and your working constraints. Then compare the evidence behind each answer. The interview should leave you with fewer assumptions to resolve in the proposal, not simply a better sales impression.

Kavita receives three confident proposals

Imagine Kavita runs a fictional music school in Varanasi. The school, owner and situation are original planning examples, not a SiteSutra client story or reported result. She wants parents to understand the courses, ask a focused question and request a trial session.

One provider talks mostly about a modern framework. Another shows an attractive restaurant website. A third promises a first place Google position. All three sound confident, but none of those statements tells Kavita who will write the course information, how enquiry delivery will be tested or what she will own after launch.

She changes the conversation. Every important claim must move through four levels: say it clearly, show relevant evidence, write the boundary and define how the finished work will be checked.

Ask six questions that produce evidence

Kavita's provider interview
QuestionUseful answer revealsRecord before approval
What visitor task are we improving?The intended audience, their decision and the primary actionOne plain language project outcome
What is included and excluded?Pages, content, integrations, review rounds and dependenciesA scope with named boundaries
What relevant evidence can I inspect?The provider's exact role, permitted work and demonstration boundariesLinks or examples with context
How will we test and accept the work?Devices, browsers, forms, accessibility, performance and release checksAn acceptance checklist and issue route
What will my business own?Domain, hosting, accounts, content, source access and handoverAn ownership and access list
What happens after launch?Support window, maintenance owner, change process and urgent contact routeA written support arrangement

A provider does not need the same process as every other company. The useful comparison is whether the answer fits the project and becomes part of the working agreement.

Start with the visitor task, not the platform

Kavita asks each provider to describe the journey in one sentence. A suitable parent should be able to confirm the course, age group, location and schedule, then request a trial session through a tested route. That sentence gives design, content and development a shared job.

If the first conversation begins with WordPress, a custom build or another platform, she asks why that choice suits editing, enquiry handling, ownership and maintenance. The platform is a consequence of those needs. It is not the business objective.

Turn “website included” into a boundary

Kavita asks who supplies course text, photographs and policy information; which pages and forms are included; how many review rounds are planned; and which external services require separate accounts or fees. She also asks what happens when a new request appears after approval.

The answer does not need to predict every change. It should distinguish a correction, a defect and new scope, then name who decides. This makes quotations more comparable without pretending that the lowest total always represents the same work.

Inspect proof without inventing a result

A useful portfolio conversation names the provider's role. Did the company design the interface, write the content, build supplied designs, configure a platform or maintain an existing site? Kavita looks for permissioned work that resembles her delivery problem, not merely her industry.

A demonstration concept can show interaction and craft, but it is not a commissioned client project or evidence of commercial results. A live client site can show current implementation, but the provider should not imply responsibility for work it did not perform. Kavita records the boundary beside every example.

Ask what “tested” means

Kavita asks for the devices, browsers and key journeys that will be checked. Her acceptance list includes navigation, readable content, keyboard access, visible focus, form validation, enquiry delivery and a mobile review. She also asks who fixes an issue found before sign off and how it will be retested.

Accessibility cannot be reduced to one automated score. The W3C recommends evaluation during development and explains that tools assist review but cannot determine accessibility by themselves. A provider should therefore describe both automated checks and relevant human checks, while being honest about the agreed scope and limitations.

Performance also needs context. Google's Web Vitals guidance separates loading, interactivity and visual stability and uses real user field data in several reporting tools. A prelaunch test can identify problems, but it cannot promise future field measurements on a new site. Kavita asks which environment was tested, which evidence will be handed over and what will be monitored later.

Replace ranking promises with search work you can inspect

If a provider promises a search position, Kavita asks for the actual work behind the statement: crawl access, descriptive pages, metadata, internal links, structured data where appropriate, a sitemap and a verified reporting property. She also asks what remains the business's responsibility, including accurate service information and useful original content.

Google's own SEO Starter Guide says that no change automatically guarantees a first place result and that some changes can take weeks or months to assess. Search visibility, AI citation samples and qualified enquiries remain separate measures. A proposal can define delivery and review; it cannot honestly guarantee a ranking or recommendation.

Write ownership before sharing access

Kavita keeps the domain and business accounts under business controlled contact details. The provider receives the minimum role needed for the agreed task. The proposal records who owns the design files, content, source or export, analytics property, Search Console property and form destination, plus what will be returned or revoked at handover.

This question is not a demand for every password. It is a request for a practical access plan. Passwords stay private; named accounts and roles make access easier to review and remove.

Open the statement closest to your proposal

These prompts turn common sales language into a useful follow up question.

The proposal says “SEO friendly”

Ask which search foundations are included, which pages receive content work, who verifies Search Console and what report is handed over. Keep ranking promises outside the acceptance criteria.

The provider shows an impressive portfolio

Ask for the provider's exact role, whether the work may be displayed and which part is relevant to your project. Do not infer client results from a screenshot.

The quote says “fully responsive and accessible”

Ask for the device and browser matrix, keyboard and focus checks, form checks, automated accessibility checks, human review scope and known limitations. Write the agreed checks into acceptance.

The lowest quote omits handover and support

Ask what you will own, what export or source is supplied, how accounts are transferred and what happens when an issue appears after launch. Compare the full working arrangement before comparing totals.

Use one scorecard for every provider

Download the web development provider interview scorecard (CSV). Use the same questions for each shortlisted provider. Record the answer, evidence, scope status, acceptance check, owner and unresolved decision.

Do not place passwords, private proposals, customer records or confidential client work in the public template. Keep sensitive material in an approved private location.

Choose the clearest working agreement

Kavita does not award points for the longest answer. She chooses the provider whose answers connect the music school's visitor task to a bounded scope, inspectable evidence, practical acceptance checks, business ownership and a support plan. Any remaining assumption becomes a written question before approval.
